items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6541

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to protecting the
confidentiality of vaccine information

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To strengthen the confidentiality protections on personal information
related to vaccines.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 amends Public Health Law § 2168 (4) (d) to provide that infor-
mation in the New York State Immunization Information System (NYSIIS)
and the New York Citywide Immunization Registry (OR) are not subject to
discovery, subpoena, warrant, or other means of legal compulsion for
release or admissible in any civil, administrative, criminal, or family
court proceeding.

§ 2 amends PHL 2168 (11) to require every effort to be made to keep
disclosure of personal identifying information from such registries
limited.

§ 3 adds a new subdivision 11-a to PHL § 2168 to state that State or
City commissioners may only share registry information with the CDC for
public health purposes and with no individually identifying information.

§ 4 creates a new PHL § 2169 on vaccine confidentiality. The new section
limits what vaccine navigators and providers can use personal informa-
tion for, and it allows them to request consent to use the information
for other purposes. It requires these entities to adhere to security
standards, and prohibits the use of the information collected from being
used to criminalize or deport an individual. The language also clarifies
that nothing in this new section will interfere with existing provider-
client, provider-patient, or familial relationships.

§ 5 amends PHL § 2180 by adding new subdivisions to define terms.

§ 6 creates a new PHL § 2183 on immunity passports. The new section
requires that providers of immunity passports, which are limited to
COVID-19, only collect the minimal amount of information required to
verify an individual's vaccine or test status, and that they delete this
information within 24 hours. It requires that any governmental entity or
public accommodation that requires proof of immunization accept physical
immunity passports, not just digital ones. It prohibits covered entities
and immunity passport providers from sharing a passport-holder's
personal information with law enforcement or in judicial proceedings,
and ensures that it cannot be used to criminalize or deport someone. It
requires the Department of Health to make regulations protecting access
to covered entities by those who are medically contraindicated from
receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, and it states that nothing in the
section shall be construed to limit a covered entity's obligations under
the Americans with Disabilities Act or any other antidiscrimination law.

§ 7 is a severability clause.

§ 8 is the immediate effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

As more New Yorkers receive the COVID-19 vaccine, it is crucial to make
sure the State and other entities that process sensitive information
about people's immunization status are protecting that data and only
using it for public health purposes. This bill strengthens the confiden-
tiality protections in the existing law on the New York State Immuniza-
tion Information System (NYSIIS) and New York Citywide Immunization
Registry (CIR), and adds in new protections for data collected by
vaccine navigators and immunity passport providers.

New York State has a long history of establishing confidentiality
protections for information gathered on people relative to contagious
diseases like HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases, and last year
we implemented confidentiality protections for the COVID-19 contact
tracing initiative. Information gathered on immunizations must also be
protected, especially as proof of immunization becomes a prerequisite
for entry to anything from sporting events to airplanes.

Before immunization passports become too ubiquitous, the state needs to
ensure that they are accessible to everyone by requiring that non-elec-
tronic versions be available and accepted, that only the minimum infor-
mation required to provide a vaccination or verify immunization status
be collected, and that no personal data be used for purposes other than
safeguarding individual and public health.  The State needs to make sure
that its efforts to promote vaccination and safely reopen the economy
don't disproportionately hurt those who have already suffered the most
during the COVID-19 pandemic. Fear of information being used to crimi-
nalize or deport a person, or take their children away, will cause some
people to avoid the vaccination and immunization passport efforts, and
could eventually inhibit their free movement in their communities. If
the State implements clear legal safeguards, however, more people will
feel comfortable engaging with these important public health initi-
atives.

This legislation preserves the confidentiality of information gathered
throughout the vaccination process. It protects individuals and provides
them with the confidence that sharing information with a vaccine provid-
er, vaccine navigator, or immunity passport provider will not put them
or their loved ones in harm's way.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER: S6541A

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to protecting the
confidentiality of vaccine information

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To strengthen the confidentiality protections on personal information
related to vaccines.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 amends PHL 2168 (11) to require that every effort to be made
to keep disclosure of individually identifiable registrant information
from the New York State Immunization Information System (NYSIIS) and the
New York Citywide Immunization Registry (OR) limited.

§ 2 adds a new subdivision 11-a to PHL § 2168 to state that State or
City commissioners may only share individually identifiable information
registrant information with CDC for public health purposes and where the
CDC has agreed not to share that information with immigration or law
enforcement agencies.

§ 3 amends Public Health Law § 2168 (4) (d) to provide that information
in the are not subject to discovery, subpoena, warrant, or other means
of legal compulsion for release or admissible in any civil, administra-
tive, criminal, or family court proceeding with narrow exceptions that
are subject to in camera review. The section also ensures that local
services districts and OCFS continue to have access to registry informa-
tion for youth in their custody.

§ 4 amends Public Health Law § 2168 (8) (b) (i) to ensure that registry
information can be used in professional misconduct proceedings.

§ 5 amends Public Health Law § 2168 (8) (c) to ensure that registry
information can be used as defense in professional misconduct
proceedings.

§ 6 creates a new PHL § 2169 on vaccine confidentiality. The new section
limits vaccine navigators to using personal information to schedule
vaccine appointments, arrange transportation to those appointments, send
reminders about appointments, and for accountability purposes and allows
navigators to request consent to use the information for other purposes.
It requires navigators to adhere to security standards and prohibits the
use of the information collected from being used to criminalize or
deport an individual. The section also prohibits vaccine providers from
requiring individuals to sign-up for bonus or loyalty card accounts as a
pre-condition to making a vaccination appointment. The language also
clarifies that nothing in this new section will interfere with existing
provider-client, provider-patient, or familial relationships.

§ 7 amends PHL § 2180 by adding new subdivisions to define terms.

§ 8 creates a new PHL § 2183 on immunity passports. The new section
requires that providers of COVID-19 immunity passports only collect the
minimal amount of information required to verify an individual's vaccine
or test status. It requires that any governmental entity or public
accommodation that requires proof of immunization accept physical immu-
nity passports, not just digital ones, and that they delete personal
information derived from an immunity passport within 24 hours - unless
the passport-holder agrees that the entity may maintain a copy of their
passport or record of their vaccination status. It prohibits covered
entities and immunity passport providers from sharing a passport-
holder's personal information with law enforcement or in judicial
proceedings, with narrow exceptions subject to in camera review, and
ensures that such information cannot be used to criminalize or deport
someone. It requires the Department of Health to make regulations
regarding reasonable accommodations for those who are medically
contraindicated from receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, and it states that
nothing in the section shall be construed to limit a covered entity's
obligations under the Americans with Disabilities Act or any other anti-
discrimination law.

§ 9 is a severability clause.

§ 10 is the immediate effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

As more New Yorkers receive the COVID-19 vaccine, it is crucial to make
sure the State and other entities that process sensitive information
about people's immunization status are protecting that data and only
using it for public health purposes. This bill strengthens the confiden-
tiality protections in the existing law on the New York State Immuniza-
tion Information System (NYSIIS) and New York Citywide Immunization

tronic versions be available and accepted, that only the minimum infor-
mation required to provide a vaccination or verify immunization status

safeguarding individual and public health.  The State needs to make sure
that its efforts to promote vaccination and safely reopen the economy
don't disproportionately hurt those who have already suffered the most
during the COVID-19 pandemic. Fear of information being used to crimi-
nalize or deport a person, or take their children away, will cause some

could eventually inhibit their free movement in their communities. If
the State implements clear legal safeguards, however, more people will
feel comfortable engaging with these important public health initi-
atives.

This legislation preserves the confidentiality of information gathered
throughout the vaccination process. It protects individuals and provides
them with the confidence that sharing information with a vaccine provid-
er, vaccine navigator, or immunity passport provider will not put them
or their loved ones in harm's way.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 107 Chapter 829
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 6541-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to  amend the public health law, in relation to protecting
        the confidentiality of vaccine information"
 
    APPROVED
 
  This  legislation  limits  the  sharing  of  immunization  information
between  the  State and the federal government and would prevent disclo-
sure of personal information related to immunization or lead  levels  in
response to any legal process, administrative action, or proceeding. The
bill  also  provides  that  absent informed consent, a vaccine navigator
shall not use, disclosure, or maintain personal  information  except  as
necessary  to  deliver an immunization. Finally, this bill would prevent
long-term storage of immunization passport information without consent.
 
  Immunizations are invaluable public  health  tools,  and  my  adminis-
tration  has  prioritized  addressing  vaccine  hesitancy throughout the
State.  Ensuring that personal information related to  immunizations  is
not  widely  shared  will  help  some  individuals feel more comfortable
taking the vaccine. However, the bill, as written, could have far-reach-
ing effects that would hinder our  ability  to  work  with  the  federal
government  to respond to public health emergencies. Without amendments,
this legislation could also hinder vaccination fraud investigations  and
prosecutions,  which  is contrary to the goals of the "Truth in Vaccina-
tion" bill I signed into law in 2021. Lastly, this  bill  would  prevent
the Department of Health from continuing its critical work to ensure our
most  vulnerable  New Yorkers are protected through vaccine mandates for
health care professionals and nursing home employees.
 
  I have reached an agreement with  the  Legislature  to  address  these
concerns,  while still ensuring there are safeguards in place to protect
individuals' identifiable information from being  disclosed  in  harmful
ways. The agreement will allow the sharing of immunization data with the
federal government when it is necessary to protect the public health, or
other  stringent  criteria are met, and will ensure that State and local
governments have the tools available  to  continue  to  address  vaccine
fraud  and mandates. As part of this agreement, identifiable information
collected from vaccine navigators will be protected from disclosure, and
any entity that requires proof of Covid-19 vaccination must also  accept
physical  proof.  On  the  basis of this agreement, I am pleased to sign
this bill into law.
 
  This bill is approved.                         (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______

summary: Restricts vaccine registry information from discovery and other process; requires the commissioner of health and the New York City commissioner of health and mental hygiene to develop regulations to protect patient vaccine information from disclosure.
